title: 23 Things I Learned Co-Editing a 650+ Page Book on Generative AI and Its Impact on Education
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: After co-editing a 650-page volume on generative AI in education, Bauschard lists 23 tentative conclusions. His central claim is that bans do not work, students are already using the tools, and schools that ignore the technology leave students unprepared. He is bullish on learning bots that provide granular one-to-one tutoring, argues teachers need professional learning on how the tools work and how to manage student use, and says AI writing detectors are unreliable. He urges educators to rethink writing standards, assessment and the skills worth teaching, and to move beyond use-it-everywhere versus ban-it debates. He warns of a widening gap between motivated students and those relying on schools, and ends with hard questions about jobs that AI will displace. The perspective is a strongly pro-integration educator's.
points: Bans are widespread in K-12 but ineffective, widening the gap between school and university and leaving students unprepared.
Granular always-available learning bots could provide the tutoring that teachers cannot give 100 students.
Teachers need professional learning that covers how LLMs work, classroom management of use, and using AI for their own workload.
AI detection tools are falsely trusted, and assessment must reduce reliance on the essay.
The real question is where, when and how to use AI, including what foundational knowledge students still need.
quotes: Many teachers and professors who have banned student use of it are quickly becoming aware that these bans do not work and that they have been forced to manage the fall out from students using it potentially inappropriately (there are more gray areas than clear cases of unethical use), producing a lot of frustration.
These are not reasons to ban the technology in schools. These are reasons to teach students about it, to properly integrate it, and to teach students to use it responsibly.

Teachers can provide many things that bots cannot, but this granular tutoring is something a teacher cannot practically provide to the 100+ students they are likely responsible for in an academic year.

Many teachers and professors falsely think “AI writing detection tools” are useful. And they falsely assume this problem (the ability of the tools to generate text output) is not going to get a lot worse
The discussion about this technology in education is focused on extremes: Use it everywhere or don’t use it at all. This isn’t helpful. The discussion needs to be about where, when and how to use it.
Students need to be educated to thrive in the world they live in, not the one we wish they (and us) live in.

Humans need to retain control of the technology and educators need to retain control over how it will be used in our space. We need to welcome the technology, but on terms that enable it to work to benefit us and our students.
